blocks.text: Strike a steel rod that is clamped at one end and it rings at close to 1 kHz; tighten a taut steel wire and its pitch rises. Both are continuous systems whose natural frequencies come straight from the speed at which a disturbance travels along them and from what happens at the ends.

blocks.markdown: A **continuous system** has mass and elasticity spread throughout, so it has infinitely many natural frequencies. For a taut string and for a straight bar vibrating along its axis the equation of motion is the same one-dimensional **wave equation**, $\partial^2u/\partial t^2=c^2\,\partial^2u/\partial x^2$, where $u(x,t)$ is displacement (m), $x$ is position along the length (m) and $c$ (m/s) is the **wave speed**. A solution with the form $u=U(x)\cos\omega t$ gives $U''+(\omega/c)^2U=0$, so $U=A\sin(\omega x/c)+B\cos(\omega x/c)$, and the boundary conditions then fix the allowed $\omega$.

blocks.title: Wave speed
blocks.text: For a taut string of tension $T$ (N) and mass per unit length $\mu$ (kg/m), transverse waves travel at $c=\sqrt{T/\mu}$. For axial (longitudinal) vibration of a slender bar of Young's modulus $E$ (Pa) and density $\rho$ (kg/m$^3$), the wave speed is $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$. Neither depends on the amplitude, and the axial speed does not depend on the cross-section or length.

blocks.markdown: **String fixed at both ends.** The boundary conditions are $U(0)=0$ and $U(L)=0$. The first gives $B=0$; the second requires $\sin(\omega L/c)=0$, so $\omega_nL/c=n\pi$ for $n=1,2,3,\dots$ The natural frequencies are therefore $f_n=nc/(2L)$ Hz, all integer multiples of the first. The mode shape $U_n=\sin(n\pi x/L)$ has $n-1$ interior nodes.

blocks.title: Frequencies of a taut steel wire
blocks.prompt: A steel wire (density 7850 kg/m^3) of diameter 1 mm is stretched with a tension of 80 N between fixed points 0.65 m apart. Find its first three natural frequencies.

steps.text: Mass per unit length from the density and area.

blocks.answer: f1 = 87.6 Hz, f2 = 175.2 Hz, f3 = 262.9 Hz (integer multiples).

blocks.markdown: **Fixed-free bar.** A bar clamped at $x=0$ and free at $x=L$ has $U(0)=0$ and, at the free end, zero axial stress, which means zero strain: $U'(L)=0$. The first condition gives $B=0$ in the solution; the second gives $(\omega/c)\cos(\omega L/c)=0$, so $\omega_nL/c=(2n-1)\pi/2$. The natural frequencies are $f_n=(2n-1)\,c/(4L)$ Hz: only **odd multiples** of the fundamental $c/(4L)$ occur. For a free-free or fixed-fixed bar the conditions give $f_n=nc/(2L)$, all integer multiples, and the fundamental is twice that of the fixed-free bar of the same length.

blocks.title: Fixed-free steel bar
blocks.prompt: A steel bar (200 GPa, 7850 kg/m^3) of length 1.2 m is clamped at one end and free at the other. Find the wave speed and the first three longitudinal natural frequencies.

steps.text: Axial wave speed depends only on the material.
Fundamental frequency: a quarter wavelength fits in the bar.
Higher frequencies are the odd multiples 3 and 5 of f_1.

items: Identify the system and its boundary conditions at each end (fixed: $U=0$; free axial end: $U'=0$).
Find the wave speed from $\sqrt{T/\mu}$ (string) or $\sqrt{E/\rho}$ (axial bar).
Apply the frequency formula for those boundary conditions.
Check dimensions: $c$ in m/s, $L$ in m, so $c/L$ is in Hz (cycles per second) before any $2\pi$ conversion.

blocks.title: What changes the frequencies
blocks.text: String: raise the tension (frequency $\propto\sqrt{T}$), shorten it ($\propto1/L$), or use a lighter wire ($\propto1/\sqrt\mu$). Axial bar: only the material ($\sqrt{E/\rho}$) and the length matter; making the bar thicker does nothing to its axial frequencies. Steel and aluminium have nearly the same $c$ (about 5000 m/s), because $E/\rho$ is almost the same for both.

blocks.title: Hz versus rad/s
blocks.text: The formulas $f_n=nc/(2L)$ and $(2n-1)c/(4L)$ give hertz. The equivalent angular frequencies are $\omega_n=2\pi f_n$: for the fixed-free bar $\omega_n=(2n-1)\pi c/(2L)$ rad/s. Do not confuse the two.

points: Strings and axially vibrating bars both obey the wave equation with speed $c=\sqrt{T/\mu}$ (string) or $c=\sqrt{E/\rho}$ (bar).
A fixed-free bar has $f_n=(2n-1)c/(4L)$ Hz: only odd multiples of the fundamental.
Free end means zero axial strain ($U'=0$); fixed end means zero displacement ($U=0$).

questions.stem: The tension in a taut string fixed at both ends is increased by a factor of four, with the length and mass per unit length unchanged. Its natural frequencies

options.text: increase by a factor of sixteen

distractorRationale.a: Correct: The wave speed is sqrt(T/mu), so quadrupling T doubles c, and f_n = n c/(2L) doubles as well.
distractorRationale.b: Frequency goes as the square root of tension, so a factor of four gives a factor of two.
distractorRationale.c: Sixteen would come from squaring the tension.
distractorRationale.d: The wave speed sqrt(T/mu) increases with tension, so frequencies change.

questions.explanation: The wave speed is sqrt(T/mu), so quadrupling T doubles c, and f_n = n c/(2L) doubles as well. Length and mass per unit length are unchanged.

questions.stem: A taut string fixed at both ends has a length of 0.45 m, a tension of 36 N and a mass per unit length of 0.004 kg/m. Find its fundamental natural frequency in Hz.
questions.explanation: The wave speed is sqrt(T/mu) = sqrt(36/0.004) = 94.87 m/s. The fundamental is c/(2L) = 94.87/(2 x 0.45) = 105.41 Hz.

questions.stem: A bar is clamped at one end and free at the other. If its fundamental longitudinal frequency is 500 Hz, which list gives its next two natural frequencies?

distractorRationale.a: That list is for a bar with both ends free or both fixed; the fixed-free bar has only odd multiples.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: For a fixed-free bar f_n = (2n-1) c/(4L), so the frequencies are 1, 3, 5 times the fundamental: 500, 1500 and 2500 Hz.
distractorRationale.c: That list is also the integer-multiple pattern of the free-free and fixed-fixed bars.
distractorRationale.d: Those are not multiples of the fundamental with the correct pattern.

questions.explanation: For a fixed-free bar f_n = (2n-1) c/(4L), so the frequencies are 1, 3, 5 times the fundamental: 500, 1500 and 2500 Hz. The free end allows a quarter-wavelength resonance but not even multiples.

questions.stem: An aluminium rod (E = 70 GPa, density 2700 kg/m^3) of length 0.8 m is clamped at one end and free at the other. Find its fundamental longitudinal natural frequency in Hz.
questions.explanation: The wave speed is sqrt(E/rho) = sqrt(7.0e10/2700) = 5092 m/s. For a fixed-free bar f_1 = c/(4L) = 5092/(4 x 0.8) = 1591 Hz.

questions.stem: A steel bar has E = 210 GPa and density 7800 kg/m^3. The speed of longitudinal waves in a slender bar of this material is about

distractorRationale.a: That multiplies by 2 pi as if converting to an angular quantity; a wave speed is not converted this way.
distractorRationale.b: That is E over rho with the square root omitted.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: The axial wave speed is c = sqrt(E/rho) = sqrt(2.10e11/7800) = 5189 m/s, using E in Pa and density in kg/m^3.
distractorRationale.d: That is the value in km/s; the unit has been confused.

questions.explanation: The axial wave speed is c = sqrt(E/rho) = sqrt(2.10e11/7800) = 5189 m/s, using E in Pa and density in kg/m^3. It does not depend on the cross-sectional area.

questions.stem: A free-free bar and a fixed-free bar are made of the same material and have the same length. How do their fundamental longitudinal frequencies compare?

options.text: They are equal, since the material and length are the same
The fixed-free bar's fundamental is twice that of the free-free bar
The free-free bar's fundamental is four times that of the fixed-free bar
The free-free bar's fundamental is twice that of the fixed-free bar

questions.correctOptionText: The free-free bar's fundamental is twice that of the fixed-free bar

distractorRationale.a: The boundary conditions change the wavelength that fits, so the frequencies differ.
distractorRationale.b: The fixed-free bar fits only a quarter wavelength, which is the lower frequency.
distractorRationale.c: The ratio is c/(2L) over c/(4L), which is two, not four.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: The free-free bar fits half a wavelength: f_1 = c/(2L).

questions.explanation: The free-free bar fits half a wavelength: f_1 = c/(2L). The fixed-free bar fits only a quarter wavelength, f_1 = c/(4L), so the free-free fundamental is twice as high.

questions.stem: The third natural frequency of a taut string fixed at both ends, of length 0.6 m and mass per unit length 0.005 kg/m, is measured as 330 Hz. Find the string tension in newtons.
questions.explanation: For a fixed-fixed string f_3 = 3c/(2L), so c = 2L f_3/3 = 2 x 0.6 x 330/3 = 132 m/s. The tension is T = mu c^2 = 0.005 x 132^2 = 87.12 N.

questions.stem: Derive the natural frequencies of a uniform bar that is fixed at one end and free at the other from the wave equation and the boundary conditions, and explain why only odd multiples of the fundamental appear.
markingGuide: Separate variables: u = U(x) cos(omega t), giving U'' + (omega/c)^2 U = 0, U = A sin(omega x/c) + B cos(omega x/c)
Fixed end at x = 0: U(0) = 0 so B = 0
Free end at x = L: zero axial force means strain U'(L) = 0, so cos(omega L/c) = 0
omega_n L/c = (2n - 1) pi/2, so omega_n = (2n - 1) pi c/(2L) rad/s and f_n = (2n - 1) c/(4L)
Mode shapes sin((2n - 1) pi x/(2L)) have a node at the fixed end and an antinode at the free end
Only odd multiples because the bar must hold an odd number of quarter wavelengths
questions.explanation: The fixed end forces a sine solution and the free end forces a cosine of the argument to vanish. The roots of cos are the odd multiples of half pi, which is why only odd multiples of the fundamental appear.

questions.stem: A designer proposes making a steel rod thicker in order to raise its longitudinal natural frequencies. Evaluate the proposal, referring to the wave speed, and say what would change the frequencies. Also compare the axial wave speed in steel (E = 200 GPa, density 7850 kg/m^3) with that in aluminium (E = 70 GPa, density 2700 kg/m^3).
markingGuide: Longitudinal frequencies depend on c = sqrt(E/rho) and L and the boundary conditions only
Cross-sectional area cancels (stiffness EA/L and mass rho A L both scale with A), so thickening has no effect on axial frequencies
Shortening the rod or choosing a material with higher E/rho raises them
Steel: sqrt(200e9/7850) is about 5048 m/s; aluminium: sqrt(70e9/2700) is about 5092 m/s, nearly equal
Therefore replacing steel by aluminium hardly changes axial frequencies, though it changes weight
Bending frequencies, unlike axial ones, do depend on the section
questions.explanation: Area appears in both the stiffness and the mass, so it cancels; the axial wave speed is a material property. Steel and aluminium have almost identical wave speeds because E/rho is nearly the same.

questions.stem: The speed of longitudinal waves in a slender uniform bar depends on the cross-sectional area of the bar.
questions.explanation: The wave speed is sqrt(E/rho), which depends only on the material properties. The cross-sectional area cancels because it appears in both the axial stiffness and the mass per unit length.
